teaching_card.title: Reading Tables and Graphs Fast (Hard)
teaching_card.body: ACT Science data questions are open-book: every answer is sitting in the table or graph. Your job is to find the right cell quickly. Read the question first, find the variable it names in the headers, locate the row or point it asks about, and only then read the number. Watch the units and the column labels; most wrong answers come from the right row in the wrong column, or the right column one row off.
key_points: Question first, then the table: know what you are hunting for.
Match the exact variable name and unit in the header before reading a value.
Put a finger on the row and a finger on the column; read where they meet.
For 'greatest' or 'least', scan one column top to bottom and mark the extreme.
A difference or ratio needs two reads; write both numbers down before combining.
Converting units? Multiply by the factor and check the size makes sense (1.2 km is 1200 m, not 12).
'Which graph matches the table?' Look at the row-to-row changes: equal steps mean a straight line.
teaching_card.worked_example: Table: 20 cm → 0.90 s, 40 cm → 1.27 s, 60 cm → 1.55 s. 'What was the period at 40 cm?' Row 40 cm, column Period: 1.27 s. Not 1.55 s (that is the next row).

screens.title: The data is the answer key
screens.body: Science passages look intimidating, but data questions do not test memory. Each one points at a specific place in a table or figure. Skim the setup for what was varied and what was measured, then go straight to the questions and let them tell you where to look.
key_points: Skim the setup: what changed, what was measured, in what units.
Do not study the whole table; let each question direct you.

screens.title: Row, column, read
screens.body: Find the question's variable in the headers. If two columns share a name (two trials, two conditions), check the label after the comma. Slide down to the row for the value in the question and read across. Common traps: the adjacent row, the other condition's column, and the value of the independent variable instead of the measured one.
key_points: Header first, then row, then the cell.
Adjacent rows and sibling columns are the usual wrong answers.

screens.title: Direction and extremes
screens.body: 'As x increased, y...' means compare each value with the one above it. If every step goes up, it increased only; if it rises then falls, say so. For 'greatest' or 'least', run a finger down one column and note the row where the extreme sits, then report that row's x value.
screens.worked_example: Period column: 0.90, 1.27, 1.55, 1.79 → every step rises, so 'increased only.' Greatest period is 1.79 s, at 80 cm.

screens.title: Two numbers, one answer
screens.body: Differences, ratios, and percent changes combine two cells. Write both values before doing arithmetic, keep track of which is first, and estimate before choosing: if 169 ÷ 64 is asked, the answer is a bit under 3, so 2.6 is plausible and 0.4 (the inverted ratio) is not.
key_points: Write both values down; then subtract or divide.
Sanity-check the size of the answer before you commit.
